title: Bracketing the Root of a Simplified Nerve-Impulse Function
context: A simplified model of a neuron's membrane-potential deviation from rest during a stimulus is given by f(V) = V^2 - 3V - 10, where V is measured in mV above resting potential and f(V) is the deviation from a target reference level. Before reaching for an iterative root-finding method, you'll first locate its roots the way Lecture 17 recommends: by inspecting a graph and checking for sign changes.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define f as an anonymous function of V. Plot f(V) over V = -6 to 8 with a grid and a reference line at y = 0 (yline). Based on the graph, report (as a comment) how many real roots f appears to have and roughly where they fall.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Evaluate f at V = -3, -1, 4, and 6 using a single fprintf-based loop (or four fprintf calls). Based on the sign of each result, state (as a comment) which of the two intervals, [-3,-1] or [4,6], brackets a root.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Factor f(V) by hand into the form (V - r1)(V - r2) and report its two exact roots as a comment. Then confirm both roots numerically using MATLAB's roots function on the coefficient vector [1 -3 -10].

starterCode:
% Problem: Bracketing the Root of a Simplified Nerve-Impulse Function
% Name:
% Date:

clear; clc; close all;

% a) Define f(V) and plot it over V = -6 to 8


% b) Evaluate f at V = -3, -1, 4, 6 and check sign changes


% c) Factor by hand (comment), then confirm with roots([1 -3 -10])
hints: A root exists somewhere between two points if f changes sign between them -- you don't need calculus to spot this, just plug in numbers and compare signs.
f is just an ordinary quadratic, so it factors the same way you would factor V^2 - 3V - 10 by hand: look for two numbers that multiply to -10 and add to -3.
Those two numbers are 5 and -2, so f(V) = (V-5)(V+2), meaning the exact roots are V = 5 and V = -2 -- check that -2 falls inside [-3,-1] and 5 falls inside [4,6].
solutionCode:
% a) Define and plot f(V)
f = @(V) V.^2 - 3*V - 10;
V = -6:0.01:8;
figure
plot(V, f(V), 'LineWidth', 2)
yline(0, 'r', 'LineWidth', 2)
xlabel('V (mV)')
ylabel('f(V)')
title('Membrane Potential Deviation Function')
grid on
% From the graph: f crosses zero twice, once near V = -2 and once near V = 5.

% b) Evaluate f at four sample points
Vtest = [-3, -1, 4, 6];
for k = 1:length(Vtest)
    fprintf('f(%d) = %.1f\n', Vtest(k), f(Vtest(k)));
end
% f(-3) = 8 (positive), f(-1) = -6 (negative) -> sign change -> root in [-3,-1]
% f(4) = -6 (negative), f(6) = 8 (positive) -> sign change -> root in [4,6]

% c) Factor by hand: V^2 - 3V - 10 = (V - 5)(V + 2) -> roots at V = 5 and V = -2
exactRoots = roots([1 -3 -10]);
disp(exactRoots)
solutionExplanation: Because f is a plain upward-opening parabola, evaluating it at a handful of points and watching the sign is enough to bracket both roots without any iterative method: f(-3) = 8 and f(-1) = -6 straddle zero, so a root must fall somewhere in between, and the same logic brackets the second root between f(4) = -6 and f(6) = 8. Factoring V^2 - 3V - 10 by hand means finding two numbers that multiply to -10 and add to -3, which are 5 and -2, giving f(V) = (V-5)(V+2) and exact roots at V = 5 and V = -2 -- both of which fall inside the intervals identified from the sign changes, and both match what roots([1 -3 -10]) reports numerically. This graphical/sign-change bracketing is exactly the reasoning Lecture 17 recommends doing before ever running Newton's method or fzero, since a good initial guess or bracket makes those methods converge faster and more reliably.
concept: Graphical root location and sign-change bracketing

context: Before fitting any nonlinear model to data, you first need an objective function that measures how well a candidate set of parameters fits. parts.label: b

parts.label: c

hints: An anonymous function can take two inputs, e.g. vmodel = @(S,c) ...; MATLAB will substitute c(1) and c(2) for Vmax and Km wherever they appear in the formula.
Since S is a vector, use element-wise operations (./ not just /) inside vmodel so it evaluates at every S value at once and returns a vector of predictions the same size as S.
SSE is just sum((predicted - measured).^2) -- square each individual error first, then add all five squared errors together into one number.
solutionExplanation: vmodel(S, c0) applies the Michaelis-Menten formula element-wise across the whole S vector at once, producing predicted rates of about [1.143, 2.000, 3.200, 4.571, 5.818] for the guess Vmax = 8, Km = 3. Comparing those against the measured v = [1.9, 3.0, 4.3, 5.4, 6.1] point by point, squaring each difference, and summing gives SSE0 approximately 3.549 -- a single number that quantifies how far off this particular guess is overall. This is exactly the quantity Lecture 19 builds an entire optimization strategy around: instead of trying to solve for Vmax and Km algebraically (which the nonlinear denominator makes impossible with ordinary linear regression), you turn the fitting problem into an optimization problem -- find the c that makes this SSE as small as possible -- which is precisely what fminsearch will be used for later in the unit.
concept: Defining a sum-of-squared-error objective function for nonlinear curve fitting

A from-scratch Newton loop needs a for or while loop that repeats x = x - f(x)/df(x) and checks the change in x against your tolerance each pass, breaking out once it's small enough.

% Date:

% b) Continue to compute x2 and x3

hints: f'(x) = 2(x-3) by the chain rule; the gradient descent update is x_(k+1) = x_k - alpha * f'(x_k), which is different from Newton's method because it never divides by the second derivative.
Apply the same update formula three times in a row, always using the previous step's output as the next step's input, exactly like you did for Newton's method earlier in the unit.

Since alpha = 0.3 is a fairly aggressive learning rate here, the iterates should approach x = 3 quickly: x1 = 1.8, x2 = 2.52, x3 = 2.808, getting closer to the true minimum at x = 3 each step but not landing exactly on it yet.

Notice the step sizes are shrinking (1.8, then 0.72, then 0.288) even though alpha never changes -- that's because the gradient itself gets smaller as x approaches the minimum at x = 3, where f'(x) = 0. fminbnd confirms the true minimum is exactly x = 3, and after only three iterations gradient descent has already closed most of the gap (2.808 vs. 3), illustrating both gradient descent's simplicity -- it never needs a second derivative like Newton's method does -- and its characteristic slow, geometric approach toward the answer rather than Newton's much faster convergence.

% b) Optimize from a reasonable initial guess

c0poor = [0.1, 1];
coptPoor = fminsearch(SSE, c0poor);
fprintf('Poor guess result: ka = %.3f, ke = %.3f, SSE = %.4f\n', coptPoor(1), coptPoor(2), SSE(coptPoor));
% In this case fminsearch converges to essentially the same optimized parameters
% as (b) despite the poor starting guess -- but this is not a guarantee for every
% nonlinear model, so a physiologically reasonable starting guess is still good practice.
solutionExplanation: fminsearch, starting from c0 = [1, 0.1], converges to ka approximately 1.491 /hr and ke approximately 0.201 /hr with a small final SSE of about 0.28, and the residual plot shows small, patternless scatter around zero rather than any systematic trend, which supports the conclusion that the one-compartment model form is a good structural match to this data rather than merely noisy. This model cannot be fit with ordinary linear regression because ka and ke each appear inside an exponential term, and those exponentials are combined by subtraction and division by their own difference (ka - ke) -- there is no algebraic rearrangement of C(t) into the y = X*beta form the normal equations require, since the parameters do not enter linearly. Refitting from a deliberately poor initial guess, c0 = [0.1, 1] (with the two rate constants effectively swapped from their expected roles), still converges to essentially the same optimized parameters here, which shows that fminsearch's Nelder-Mead simplex search can sometimes recover from a bad starting point for well-behaved problems like this one -- but this is not a guarantee in general, since more complex or more parameter-heavy SSE surfaces can have multiple local minima that trap a poorly chosen initial guess, which is why picking a physiologically plausible starting point remains good practice even when it isn't strictly required.
concept: Nonlinear pharmacokinetic model fitting, residual diagnostics, and initial-guess sensitivity

title: Distinguishing a True Extremum from an Inflection Point: Root-Finding vs. Optimization
context: A stationary point of an objective function (where the derivative is zero) is a necessary condition for an extremum, but it isn't sufficient -- a root of f'(x) can also be an inflection point where the function briefly flattens without actually turning around. This problem explores that subtlety using f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3 + 2 (a normalized model of cumulative tissue strain relative to a loading parameter x), over x in [-1,4], and compares finding critical points via root-finding on f' against finding the minimum directly with fminbnd.

If it is inconclusive, compute the third derivative symbolically, evaluate it at x = 0, and use Lecture 18's higher-order-derivative rule (first nonzero derivative of even order means an extremum; odd order means an inflection point) to classify x = 0.

In 3-5 sentences (as a comment or printed string), reconcile all of your findings: why fzero applied to f', started near x = 0, still converges to the other critical point instead, why the classification at x = 0 needed a third derivative, and how fminbnd's result relates to the critical point fzero found.

hints: f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3 + 2 gives f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2, which factors as 4x^2(x-3) -- notice x = 0 is a repeated (double) root of f', while x = 3 is a simple root.

fzero relies on detecting a sign change to bracket a root; since f'(x) = 4x^2(x-3) never actually changes sign at x = 0 (x^2 is never negative), fzero has essentially nothing to grab onto there and will instead wander to the nearby simple root at x = 3, even from a starting guess close to 0.

When f''(x*) = 0 the second-derivative test is inconclusive by itself; Lecture 18 says to keep differentiating until you hit a nonzero derivative, then check whether its order is even (extremum) or odd (inflection point) -- here f'''(x) = 24x - 24, so f'''(0) = -24, a nonzero third derivative, meaning x = 0 is an inflection point, not an extremum at all.
solutionExplanation: Factoring f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 as 4x^2(x-3) shows x = 0 is a double root and x = 3 is a simple root; evaluating the second derivative f''(x) = 12x^2 - 24x at x = 0 gives exactly 0, so Lecture 18's ordinary second-derivative test is inconclusive there, and only a nonzero third derivative (f'''(0) = -24, an odd order) resolves the ambiguity by classifying x = 0 as an inflection point rather than a true extremum. Running fzero on f' from two different nonzero starting guesses, x0 = 0.5 and x0 = -0.5, both converge to x = 3 instead of x = 0 -- this is a direct consequence of fzero's reliance on sign changes to bracket a root, and since x^2 never goes negative, f' never actually changes sign at its double root, giving fzero nothing to bracket there even from very close starting points. At x = 3, the ordinary second-derivative test is perfectly conclusive: f''(3) = 36 > 0 confirms a genuine local minimum. fminbnd, applied directly to f(x) over [-1,4] without ever touching a derivative, independently converges to the same x = 3, tying the whole exercise together: root-finding on the derivative and direct optimization agree on the true minimum, but only fzero's very mechanism for finding roots happened to protect it from being confused by the non-extremal critical point at x = 0 -- a protection that direct differentiation-based reasoning needed a third derivative to achieve.

title: Fitting Substrate-Inhibition Enzyme Kinetics and Justifying the Nonlinear Approach
context: In enzyme kinetics, substrate inhibition occurs when an excess of substrate actually reduces the reaction rate instead of continuing to increase it, unlike ordinary Michaelis-Menten behavior. The rate v as a function of substrate concentration [S] is modeled as v([S]) = Vmax*[S] / (Km + [S] + [S]^2/Ki). You're given experimental data spanning two orders of magnitude in substrate concentration and asked to fit Vmax, Km, and Ki, then justify your choice of fitting method.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Given S = [0.2 0.5 1 2 4 8 16 32] and v = [0.9 2.0 3.4 5.0 6.0 5.3 3.8 2.1], define the substrate-inhibition model as an anonymous function vmodel(S,c) with c = [Vmax, Km, Ki].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Define the SSE objective function and use fminsearch with the initial guess c0 = [7, 1, 20] to estimate the three parameters. Display Vmax, Km, and Ki rounded to 3 decimal places, along with the initial and final SSE.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot the data and fitted curve on a semilogx plot, since the substrate concentrations span two orders of magnitude.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Compute the residuals (v minus the model prediction) and plot them against S (using semilogx for the x-axis again). Based on the pattern (or lack of pattern), state in a comment whether the model appears to be a good structural fit.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: In 3-5 sentences (as a comment or printed string), explain why this substrate-inhibition model cannot be linearized the way ordinary Michaelis-Menten kinetics can (via a Lineweaver-Burk 1/v vs. 1/[S] plot), and why fminsearch on the raw SSE is the appropriate tool here instead.

% Problem: Fitting Substrate-Inhibition Enzyme Kinetics and Justifying the Nonlinear Approach
% Name:
% Date:

S = [0.2 0.5 1 2 4 8 16 32];
v = [0.9 2.0 3.4 5.0 6.0 5.3 3.8 2.1];

% a) Define vmodel(S,c)


% b) Define SSE(c) and fminsearch from c0 = [7, 1, 20]


% c) semilogx plot of data and fitted curve


% d) Residuals vs. S


% e) Written explanation (comment or string)
hints: vmodel should use c(1) for Vmax, c(2) for Km, and c(3) for Ki inside the substrate-inhibition formula -- remember to use element-wise operations (./ and .^) since S is a vector.

semilogx(x, y) plots y on a normal linear axis but stretches x onto a logarithmic scale, which is exactly what you want when your independent variable (S here) spans from 0.2 to 32 -- use it for both the raw data plot and the residual plot.

Look at the algebraic form: Km, [S], and [S]^2/Ki are all added together in the denominator underneath a single Vmax*[S] numerator -- there is no way to take a reciprocal of both sides and get a clean straight-line relationship the way you can for the simpler Km + [S] denominator in ordinary Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
solutionCode:
% a) Define the substrate-inhibition model
S = [0.2 0.5 1 2 4 8 16 32];
v = [0.9 2.0 3.4 5.0 6.0 5.3 3.8 2.1];
vmodel = @(S,c) c(1)*S ./ (c(2) + S + S.^2/c(3));

% b) Define SSE and optimize
SSE = @(c) sum((vmodel(S,c) - v).^2);
c0 = [7, 1, 20];
copt = fminsearch(SSE, c0);
fprintf('Vmax = %.3f, Km = %.3f, Ki = %.3f\n', copt(1), copt(2), copt(3));
fprintf('Initial SSE = %.4f, Final SSE = %.4f\n', SSE(c0), SSE(copt));

% c) semilogx plot of data and fitted curve
Sfine = logspace(log10(0.1), log10(40), 300);
figure
semilogx(S, v, 'ko', 'MarkerFaceColor', 'k', 'MarkerSize', 8)
hold on
semilogx(Sfine, vmodel(Sfine, copt), 'r-', 'LineWidth', 2)
xlabel('Substrate Concentration, [S] (mM)')
ylabel('Reaction Rate, v')
title('Substrate-Inhibition Kinetics Fit')
legend('Data', 'Fitted Curve', 'Location', 'northeast')
grid on
hold off

% d) Residuals vs. S
resid = v - vmodel(S, copt);
figure
semilogx(S, resid, 'bo-', 'LineWidth', 1.5, 'MarkerFaceColor', 'b')
yline(0, 'k--')
xlabel('Substrate Concentration, [S] (mM)')
ylabel('Residual (Data - Model)')
title('Residuals vs. Substrate Concentration')
grid on
% The residuals are small and show no obvious systematic trend across S, supporting
% the substrate-inhibition model as a good structural fit rather than just noisy data.

% e) Written explanation
explanation = ['Ordinary Michaelis-Menten kinetics can be linearized because its ' ...
    'denominator is just Km + [S], so taking the reciprocal of both sides of ' ...
    'v = Vmax*[S]/(Km+[S]) produces 1/v = (Km/Vmax)*(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, a straight ' ...
    'line in 1/[S] (the Lineweaver-Burk plot). Here, the denominator has an extra ' ...
    '[S]^2/Ki term, so taking the reciprocal produces 1/v = (Km/(Vmax*[S])) + ' ...
    '1/Vmax + [S]/(Vmax*Ki), which still has an [S] term on the right-hand side ' ...
    'even after inverting -- there is no substitution that turns this into a ' ...
    'straight line in any single transformed variable. Because no linearizing ' ...
    'transformation exists, ordinary linear regression and the normal equations ' ...
    'are not an option here, which is exactly why fminsearch on the raw SSE -- ' ...
    'comparing the untransformed model directly against the untransformed data -- ' ...
    'is the appropriate and, in this case, necessary tool.'];
disp(explanation)
solutionExplanation: fminsearch, started from the guess [7, 1, 20], converges to approximately Vmax = 15.295, Km = 3.327, Ki = 5.488, reducing the SSE from about 2.754 at the initial guess to about 0.025 at the optimum -- a fit tight enough that the residual plot in part (d) shows only small, patternless scatter around zero across the full two-decade range of substrate concentrations, supporting the substrate-inhibition model as structurally appropriate rather than merely a noisy fit. The reason this model resists the classic Lineweaver-Burk linearization trick used for ordinary Michaelis-Menten kinetics is entirely algebraic: ordinary Michaelis-Menten's denominator, Km + [S], inverts cleanly into a straight line in 1/[S], but the substrate-inhibition denominator's extra [S]^2/Ki term means that after inverting, an [S] term is still present on the right-hand side alongside the 1/[S] term, so no single reciprocal transformation collapses the relationship into anything linear. With no linearizing substitution available, the normal equations approach used for linear regression simply isn't applicable, which is precisely the situation Lecture 19 designs the SSE-plus-fminsearch approach to handle -- any nonlinear model, linearizable or not, can be fit by minimizing its sum of squared errors directly.
concept: Fitting a substrate-inhibition kinetic model and justifying nonlinear least squares over linearization
